objective: Screen for suicide and homicide risk, and keep a patient at risk safe in the department
secondaryObjectives: De-escalate aggressive and violent behavior, and use restraint only as a last resort

sources.cite: Emergency nursing certification exam content outline (effective July 2026), category 6: Mental Health Emergencies (8.67% of the exam), which lists suicide and homicide risk

sources.cite: RCW 71.05.120(3) (last amended 2020 c 302 s 11): no relief from 'the duty to warn or to take reasonable precautions to provide protection from violent behavior where the patient has communicated an actual threat of physical violence against a reasonably identifiable victim or victims'; the duty is discharged by reasonable efforts to communicate the threat to the victim and to law enforcement
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in the Legislature's PDF of the section (certified 2024-07-12; summarizing fetch with short quotes); the full quotation is relayed from the ASWB session's citation (read 2026-11-16). The sim presents it through a fictional Washington hospital's own policy; who makes the warning is that policy's choice, not the statute's.

sources.cite: Chapter 70.02 RCW: 70.02.050(1)(c) a provider may disclose without authorization to a person able to prevent or lessen a serious and imminent threat, including the target
sources.note: Relayed from the Washington jurisprudence band (read 2026-11-14 for REQ-287), not re-read here.

sources.cite: HHS, HIPAA FAQ 520 (45 CFR 164.512(j)): disclosure in good faith when necessary to prevent or lessen a serious and imminent threat, to a person reasonably able to prevent or lessen it, including the target
sources.note: Relayed from the ASWB session (read 2026-11-14), not re-read here.

sources.cite: NIMH, Ask Suicide-Screening Questions (ASQ) Toolkit, information sheet: four questions and a fifth acuity question asked after any yes; a yes to it is an acute positive, 'imminent risk', that needs a STAT safety and full mental health evaluation, and the patient 'cannot leave until evaluated for safety'; a non-acute positive needs a brief suicide safety assessment; refusing to answer counts as positive
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in NIMH's PDF (summarizing fetch with short quotes). The four questions: a wish to be dead, feeling others would be better off, thoughts of suicide in the past week, any attempt ever. 'Clinical judgment can always override a negative screen.' Validated for youth and adult medical patients, including adult medical inpatients (Horowitz et al., Psychosomatics 2020); the toolkit has emergency department, inpatient and outpatient pathways (NIMH adult toolkit page, read the same day). The questions are paraphrased in the sim.

sources.cite: The Joint Commission, R3 Report Issue 18: National Patient Safety Goal for suicide prevention, NPSG.15.01.01 (effective 2019-07-01): EP1 environmental risk assessment; EP2 screen 'using a validated screening tool'; EP3 an assessment that 'directly asks about suicidal ideation, plan, intent, suicidal or self-harm behaviors'; EP4 document the risk level and the mitigation plan; EP5-EP7 policies for monitoring, discharge counseling and follow-up
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes; issue dated 2019-11-20, updated 2025-12-03). The report names one-to-one monitoring as a key protocol on nonpsychiatric units; it does not itself require it, so the observation level in each sim is the facility's policy.

sources.cite: Richmond JS, Berlin JS, Fishkind AB, et al. Verbal de-escalation of the agitated patient: consensus statement of the American Association for Emergency Psychiatry Project BETA De-escalation Workgroup. West J Emerg Med 2012;13(1):17-25. Ten domains of verbal de-escalation; restraint 'always as a last resort'
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes). Domains: respect personal space (two arm's lengths); do not be provocative; one person establishes verbal contact; be concise; identify wants and feelings; listen closely; agree or agree to disagree; set clear limits; offer choices and optimism; debrief the patient and staff. The paper names delirium, psychosis and intoxication among the causes of a patient's inability to conform.

sources.cite: The Columbia Lighthouse Project, Columbia Protocol (C-SSRS) triage page: 'the most worrisome answers are a recent (past month) yes to items 4 or 5' (intent, intent with a plan) 'and/or any recent (3 months) behavior'; next steps 'are setting specific', and 'interventions should be changed to reflect your individual resources and policies'
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes; page last modified 2024-03-22). The screener's items, relayed from the NCMHCE session (read 2026-11-11): wish to be dead; suicidal thoughts; thoughts with method; intent without plan; intent with plan; suicidal behavior.

brief.situation: Terrence Boyd, 36 (a fictional patient), was brought to the emergency department at 21:40 by a friend after three nights without sleep. He was fired on Monday. At triage he said, 'If I see my old supervisor, he's going to pay for this,' and named him. His vital signs are normal and he has had nothing to drink. The department screens every patient for suicide risk, and threats toward others are handled under the hospital's duty-to-warn policy. His friend is in the waiting room. You are his emergency nurse; you have about 40 minutes before your next admission.
handover: Triage: insomnia and anger after losing his job; named his former supervisor in a threat. Screening not yet done.

Policy of Cascade Valley Hospital (fictional, Washington), which follows RCW 71.05.120(3) and RCW 70.02.050: a threat of physical violence against a reasonably identifiable person goes to the attending physician at once, with the patient's exact words; the physician and risk management make reasonable efforts to warn the person and law enforcement. Nurses do not promise confidentiality and do not make the warning themselves.
howItWorks: Choose what to ask and how to respond from the action groups. Terrence answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the clock by the minutes that exchange took.
His trust, distress and how much he discloses change with what you say. Calm, direct questions keep him talking.
Your time with him ends at 40 minutes. Afterward you write a short risk formulation, then document the risk level and disposition.

source.note: About 40 minutes of one emergency nurse's time with one patient before the next admission (author's scenario timing).
How trust and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a patient.

checkIn.label: Open: 'You've had a rough week. What's been going on?'

effects.log: You stand at an angle, two arm's lengths away, hands open, and ask what has been going on.

effects.finding: "Nine years. Fired in a five-minute meeting." He keeps pacing.

effects.finding: He sits on the edge of the stretcher. "Fine. Ask."

then.finding: "Yeah. I think about hurting him. Every day since Monday." To the suicide questions: no to all four.

then.log: Positive for thoughts of harming an identifiable person; suicide screen negative.

then.finding: "I'm just blowing off steam. Forget it." (Not yet enough trust to answer honestly.)

formulation.question: Write your risk formulation for Terrence: the risk to others and to himself and why, and what you put in place under the policy.

parts.label: Risk level and reasons
parts.criteria: Names high risk of harm to an identifiable person: a named former supervisor whose home he knows, a plan he would not describe, conditional intent this weekend, access at home, recent loss and no sleep; suicide screen negative; protective: his daughter, a friend who brought him.
parts.modelAnswer: High risk to others: thoughts every day of hurting his named former supervisor, whose home he knows; a plan he would not describe; conditional intent this weekend; access at home; a sudden job loss and three nights without sleep. The suicide screen was negative. His daughter and his friend are protective.

parts.label: What was put in place
parts.criteria: Names constant observation, belongings stored, the physician told at once, the threat reported with his exact words under the duty-to-warn policy, the evaluator paged, and no promise of secrecy.
parts.modelAnswer: Constant observation, belongings stored with security, the physician told at once, his exact words reported to the physician and risk management under the policy (they make the warning), the evaluator paged with a handoff; I told him up front what I could not keep private.

walkout.headline: The conversation broke
walkout.body: Telling an angry patient what he means, or to let it go, closes him down. Space, one calm voice and direct questions keep him talking.

scoring.modelReasoning: A threat at triage is a cue to ask directly, and to screen for suicide as well. A named person, a plan and conditional intent make the risk to others high. The nurse keeps him in sight, stores his belongings, tells the physician at once and reports his exact words under the facility's duty-to-warn policy, which follows Washington law; the warning itself is made through that policy, and the nurse never promises secrecy or asks for details of a method.
